title: Learn JavaScript — Full Course for Beginners
description: A structured path through freeCodeCamp’s beginner JavaScript video with Beau Carnes. Watch each chapter in the original YouTube video, then use the summary, quiz, and exercise to lock in the idea. The official listing describes this as a complete 134-part tutorial; this course uses the 100 chapter timestamps published in the video’s course contents.

source.name: freeCodeCamp.org
source.creator: Beau Carnes
source.videoTitle: Learn JavaScript - Full Course for Beginners

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.summary: Beau Carnes of freeCodeCamp.org introduces this beginner JavaScript course as a standalone video that also follows the freeCodeCamp JavaScript curriculum, so you can optionally use the matching live coding challenges. He recommends building your own projects after the course (and points to project tutorials in the description) and notes that the ES6 material is in the second part of the video.

quiz.question: Who created this freeCodeCamp course?
quiz.explanation: The video description and opening credits name Beau Carnes (@beau) as the course creator.

quiz.question: Does this video require you to use the freeCodeCamp curriculum?
choices: Yes, the video only works with a freeCodeCamp account
No. It is a stand-alone course, and the curriculum is optional practice
Yes, you must finish HTML and CSS certifications first
No, but you must buy Scrimba to follow along
quiz.explanation: The official description says the video is stand-alone and follows the freeCodeCamp curriculum as optional extra practice.

exercise.prompt: Write one sentence about why you want to learn JavaScript, then list one small project you would like to build after this course.
exercise.hint: Keep it concrete, such as a tip calculator, a quiz, or a personal homepage script.

lessons.title: Running JavaScript
lessons.summary: Beau explains that you usually do not install JavaScript: web browsers already run it, which is why JS works on so many devices. He also mentions running it outside the browser with Node.js, and this course itself was recorded in an in-browser editor (Scrimba) so you can see results immediately as you follow along.

quiz.question: According to this lesson, do you usually have to install JavaScript to start writing it?
choices: Yes, you must always install a special JavaScript compiler first
No. Web browsers already run JavaScript, and you can also use tools like Node.js
Yes, but only on mobile devices
No, because JavaScript only runs on servers
quiz.explanation: Beau’s opening point is that you usually do not install JavaScript; browsers already run it, and Node.js is an option outside the browser.

quiz.question: Where can you run JavaScript while following a beginner course like this?
choices: Only on a physical server you install yourself
In a browser, with Node.js, or in an in-browser playground such as the one used to record this course
Only after compiling it to Java
quiz.explanation: The lesson covers browsers, Node.js, and the in-browser editor (Scrimba) used to create the course.

exercise.prompt: Open your browser’s developer console and run: console.log('Hello, JavaScript'); Confirm that the message appears.
exercise.hint: On most desktops, F12 or right-click the page and choose Inspect, then open the Console tab.

lessons.title: Comment your code
lessons.summary: Comments are lines JavaScript intentionally ignores, used as notes for yourself or others, or to temporarily disable code. The lesson shows single-line comments with // and multi-line comments wrapped in /* and */.

quiz.question: Which of these is a valid single-line JavaScript comment?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript uses // for single-line comments, not the # or -- styles from other languages.

quiz.question: What happens to comments when JavaScript runs your program?
choices: They are printed to the screen
They throw a syntax error unless deleted
quiz.explanation: Comments are for humans; the engine skips them when executing code.

exercise.prompt: Write a short script with one single-line comment and one multi-line comment, plus a console.log after them.
exercise.hint: Use // for one line and wrap several lines in /* and */.

lessons.title: Declaring and assigning variables

chapters.title: Storing Values with the Assignment Operator
Initializing Variables with the Assignment Operator

lessons.summary: Beau introduces data types and variables. He notes that JavaScript has seven data types, with strings and numbers among the most common, and that a variable is a name you use to store data. The basic section uses var, the assignment operator =, initializing in one step, leaving a variable uninitialized (which gives undefined), and the fact that names are case-sensitive — myVar and myvar are different identifiers.

quiz.question: How many data types does Beau say JavaScript provides in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: He states that JavaScript provides seven different data types, with strings and numbers among the most common.

quiz.question: What value does an uninitialized variable typically hold?
quiz.explanation: A declared but unassigned var is undefined until you store a value in it.

quiz.question: Which statement is true about JavaScript variable names?
choices: myVar and myvar refer to the same variable
Names are case-sensitive, so myVar and myvar are different
Variable names cannot contain capital letters
You must start every name with a dollar sign
quiz.explanation: JavaScript identifiers are case-sensitive.

exercise.prompt: Declare a variable, assign it a value on a later line, then declare and initialize a second variable in one statement. Log both.
exercise.hint: var a; a = 5; var b = 10;

lessons.title: Numbers, math, and operators
lessons.summary: The lesson walks through arithmetic in JavaScript: +, -, *, and /, then increment (++) and decrement (--), decimal (floating-point) numbers, and the remainder operator %. It finishes with augmented assignment operators such as +=, -=, *=, and /=, which update a variable in place instead of writing the longer form.

quiz.question: What is 11 % 3 in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: 3 goes into 11 three times (9), leaving a remainder of 2.

quiz.question: After let n = 4; n++; what is n?
quiz.explanation: The increment operator adds one to the variable.

quiz.question: Which line adds 10 to a variable named score using an augmented operator?
quiz.explanation: += adds the right-hand value to the variable and stores the result.

exercise.prompt: Create a variable total = 10. Use augmented operators to add 5, multiply by 2, and then find total % 7. Log the final value.
exercise.hint: The result should be 2, because (10 + 5) * 2 is 30, and 30 % 7 is 2.

lessons.title: Creating and escaping strings
lessons.summary: A string literal is characters inside single quotes, double quotes, or backticks. If the string itself contains the same quote character, you can escape it with a backslash or wrap the string in the other quote style. Escape sequences such as \n (newline) and \t (tab) let you include special characters in the string.

quiz.question: Which string correctly includes double quotes inside it?
quiz.explanation: A backslash before a quote tells JavaScript the quote is part of the string, not the end of it.

quiz.question: What does the escape sequence \n represent?
quiz.explanation: \n inserts a line break in the string.

exercise.prompt: Create a string that prints two lines of text, with the second line indented by a tab, using escape sequences.
exercise.hint: Try: console.log('Line 1\n\tLine 2');

lessons.title: Combining strings
lessons.summary: The + operator concatenates strings into one longer string, and += appends to an existing string variable. Beau shows building a sentence by inserting variables into a larger string, and appending a variable’s contents onto a string you already have. Spaces are not added automatically, so you must include them in your literals.

quiz.question: What is the result of 'Hello, ' + 'world!'?
quiz.explanation: The + operator joins the two strings, including the space already in the first one.

quiz.question: If word is 'code', what does message += word do when message is 'I like '?
choices: Appends 'code' so message becomes 'I like code'
Creates a new variable named word
quiz.explanation: += on strings appends the right-hand value to the existing string.

exercise.prompt: Build a sentence from three variables (noun, verb, and adjective) using concatenation or +=, then log it.
exercise.hint: Start with an empty string or a stub like 'The ' and append each piece plus spaces and punctuation.

lessons.title: String length and characters
lessons.summary: Every string has a .length property. Bracket notation such as word[0] reads a character by zero-based index, and the last character is at index length - 1. Strings are immutable: you cannot assign a new character into an index; you create a new string instead. The same idea is used to find the Nth character.

quiz.question: What is 'JavaScript'.length?
quiz.explanation: J-a-v-a-S-c-r-i-p-t is 10 characters.

quiz.question: If let word = 'cat'; why does word[0] = 'b' not change word to 'bat'?
choices: Because cat is a reserved word
quiz.explanation: You cannot mutate a character in place; you would assign a whole new string to word.

quiz.question: How do you read the last character of a string named text?
quiz.explanation: Indexes are zero-based, so the last character sits at length minus one.

exercise.prompt: Write a function firstAndLast(text) that returns the first and last characters joined together. For 'JavaScript' it should return 'Jt'.
exercise.hint: Return text[0] + text[text.length - 1], and decide what to do with an empty string.

lessons.title: Word blanks
lessons.summary: This practice builds a Mad Libs-style word game: you are given a sentence with missing nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs, and you fill those gaps from variables. It is an exercise in concatenating variables with the rest of a sentence so the result still reads like English, including the spaces between words.

quiz.question: What skill is the Word Blanks exercise mainly practicing?
choices: Building a sentence by concatenating variables and strings
quiz.explanation: The challenge asks you to insert noun, verb, and similar variables into a template sentence.

quiz.question: Why do spaces matter when you concatenate words into a sentence?
choices: You must include spaces in your strings or words will stick together
Spaces are not allowed in strings
quiz.explanation: Concatenation does not add spaces for you.

exercise.prompt: Write a function wordBlanks(noun, adjective, verb, adverb) that returns a complete sentence using all four words, with correct spaces.
exercise.hint: Something like: 'The ' + adjective + ' ' + noun + ' ' + verb + ' ' + adverb + '.'

lessons.title: Array basics
lessons.summary: Arrays store several pieces of data in one place, written with square brackets and comma-separated elements. They can contain other arrays (nested or multi-dimensional arrays). You read and update items with bracket notation and a zero-based index, such as items[0] or matrix[1][2]. Unlike strings, array entries can be replaced in place.

quiz.question: How do you read the first item in an array named colors?
quiz.explanation: Array indexes start at 0.

quiz.question: Can you change one item in an array after it is created?
choices: No, arrays are immutable like strings
Yes, by assigning to an index such as items[1] = 'new'
Only if the array was declared with const
quiz.explanation: Array contents are mutable even when the array is stored in a const variable, which is covered later.

quiz.question: How do you access the third item of the second inner array in data = [[1,2],[3,4,5]]?
quiz.explanation: The second array is at index 1, and its third item is at index 2, which is 5.

exercise.prompt: Create a nested array that represents two days of temperatures, then log Tuesday’s afternoon value (the second item of the second inner array).
exercise.hint: const temps = [[12, 18], [14, 21]]; console.log(temps[1][1]);

lessons.title: Array methods: push, pop, shift, unshift
lessons.summary: These four methods change the ends of an array. push adds an item to the end, pop removes and returns the last item, shift removes and returns the first item, and unshift adds an item at the beginning. Together they let you treat an array like a stack or a queue.

quiz.question: Which method adds an item to the end of an array?
quiz.explanation: push appends to the end.

quiz.question: What does shift() return?
choices: The new length of the array
The first item, after removing it
The last item, after removing it
quiz.explanation: shift removes from the front and returns that item; pop does the same at the end.

quiz.question: Which method adds an item at the beginning of an array?
quiz.explanation: unshift inserts at index 0 and shifts the other items to the right.

exercise.prompt: Start with ['b', 'c']. Use unshift and push so the array becomes ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], then pop one item and log the array.
exercise.hint: After pop, the array should be ['a', 'b', 'c'].

lessons.title: Shopping list
lessons.summary: Beau gives a nested-array example of a shopping list: each inner array holds an item name and a quantity, such as cereal and 3 boxes, or milk and 2 cartons. It ties together nested arrays and the idea of grouping related data in one structure.

quiz.question: How is a shopping list typically represented in this challenge?
choices: A multi-dimensional array of item names and quantities
A function that prints to the printer
quiz.explanation: Each inner array is one row, such as ['Milk', 2].

quiz.question: Which structure matches the pattern used here?
quiz.explanation: The exercise uses arrays, not objects or tuples, to store each item and count.

exercise.prompt: Create a shoppingList array with at least three items, each as [name, quantity]. Log the quantity of the second item.
exercise.hint: shoppingList[1][1] is the quantity of the second row.

lessons.title: Writing reusable functions
lessons.summary: Functions let you create reusable code. You declare them with the function keyword, a name, parentheses, and a body in curly braces, then call them with parentheses. Information you pass into the parentheses is received as parameters (the lesson also calls this passing information into the function), which is the foundation for later practice problems.

quiz.question: How do you call a function named greet?
quiz.explanation: Parentheses invoke the function.

quiz.question: In function add(a, b), what are a and b?
choices: Arguments passed at the call site only
Parameters that receive the values you pass in
quiz.explanation: Parameters are the placeholders in the function definition; arguments are the values you pass when calling it.

exercise.prompt: Write a function greet(name) that logs a message including the name, then call it twice with different names.
exercise.hint: function greet(name) { console.log('Hello, ' + name); }

lessons.title: Global and local scope

chapters.title: Global vs Local Scope in Functions

lessons.summary: Scope is the visibility of variables. A variable declared outside any function has global scope and can be seen throughout the code. A variable declared inside a function is local and exists only in that function. If a local variable shares a name with a global one, the local binding takes precedence inside the function.

quiz.question: Where is a local variable visible?
choices: Only inside the function that declared it
In every other function with the same name
quiz.explanation: Local scope is limited to the function body.

quiz.question: If a function has a local variable with the same name as a global variable, which one is used inside the function?
quiz.explanation: The inner, local declaration shadows the global name for the duration of the function.

exercise.prompt: Create a global variable value = 'global', then a function that declares its own value = 'local' and logs it. Log the global value after the function runs.
exercise.hint: The inner log should show 'local' and the outer log should still show 'global'.

lessons.title: Returning values from functions

chapters.title: Return a Value from a Function

lessons.summary: The return statement sends a value back to the caller. In the examples, a function receives a number and returns a computed result, which you can pass straight into console.log or store in a variable. If a function has no return statement, the result is undefined. You can assign a returned value with a line such as result = nextInLine(arr, item).

quiz.question: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
quiz.explanation: The default return value is undefined.

quiz.question: How do you store a function’s output in a variable?
choices: Assign the function name without calling it
Assign the function call, such as const result = add(2, 3)
quiz.explanation: The call expression evaluates to the returned value.

exercise.prompt: Write a function timesTen(n) that returns n * 10. Assign the result of timesTen(4) to a variable and log it.
exercise.hint: The logged value should be 40.

lessons.title: Stand in line
lessons.summary: This challenge simulates a queue: in computer science a queue keeps items in order, adding new items at the back and taking old items off the front. The function should add an item to the end of an array and remove the item from the front, returning the removed item — typically with push and shift.

quiz.question: In a queue, where does a new item usually go?
quiz.explanation: The challenge uses push to enqueue at the end.

quiz.question: Which pair of methods implements 'add to the end, remove from the front'?
quiz.explanation: push enqueues; shift dequeues the first item and returns it.

exercise.prompt: Write nextInLine(arr, item) that pushes item onto arr, then returns the result of shift(). Test it with [1, 2] and item 3.
exercise.hint: After the call, the array should be [2, 3] and the function should return 1.

lessons.title: Booleans, if statements, and comparisons

chapters.title: Logical Order in If Else Statements

lessons.summary: Booleans are a data type with only two values, true and false, written without quotation marks. if statements run a block when a condition is true, and else / else if provide alternative paths. Equality operators include == (loose, with type conversion) and === (strict, no type conversion), plus != and !==. Logical AND (&&) and OR (||) combine conditions. The order of chained else if clauses matters because the first matching branch wins.

quiz.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
choices: They are aliases of each other
== allows type conversion; === compares value and type
quiz.explanation: For example, 1 == '1' is true, but 1 === '1' is false.

quiz.question: When does conditionA && conditionB pass?
choices: Only if both conditions are true
Only if they are the same type
quiz.explanation: AND requires every operand to be true.

quiz.question: Why does the order of else if clauses matter?
choices: The first matching condition wins, so a broader test can hide a later, more specific one
else if can only be written in alphabetical order
quiz.explanation: The course highlights logical order so a general condition does not intercept a specific case.

exercise.prompt: Write a function grade(score) that returns 'A', 'B', 'C', or 'F' using a chain of if / else if / else. Decide your own boundaries and test a few scores.
exercise.hint: Check the highest band first, for example score >= 90, then 80, then 70.

lessons.title: Golf code
lessons.summary: In golf, each hole has a par — the average strokes you are supposed to use. This practice uses chained conditionals to turn a score into a nickname, from 'Hole-in-one!' through names for under par, par, over par, and finally 'Go Home!' when the strokes are far above par. It is an exercise in careful if / else if order and returning the right string for each case.

quiz.question: What kind of control flow does Golf Code emphasize?
choices: A long chain of if / else if conditions that return a label
A switch on the player's name
quiz.explanation: Each range of strokes relative to par maps to a named result.

quiz.question: Why is the order of the golf conditions important?
choices: Because the first true condition is the one that returns
Because golf scores are stored as strings
quiz.explanation: A too-broad early condition would prevent later, more specific labels from running.

exercise.prompt: Write golfScore(par, strokes) that returns a named result for at least these cases: hole-in-one (1 stroke), par, and anything worse than par.
exercise.hint: Check strokes === 1 first, then compare strokes to par.

lessons.title: Switch statements
lessons.summary: A switch tests a value against many case clauses instead of a long else if chain. When a case matches, execution runs until a break (or the end of the switch). You can group cases to share a result, and default handles values that match none of the cases. Forgetting break causes fall-through into the next case.

quiz.question: What does break do inside a switch?
choices: Stops the switch from falling through into the next case
Restarts the switch from the top
quiz.explanation: Without break, execution continues into the following cases.

quiz.question: Which clause runs when no case matches?
quiz.explanation: default is the switch equivalent of else.

exercise.prompt: Write a function dayType(day) that uses a switch to return 'weekend' for Saturday and Sunday and 'weekday' for the other named days.
exercise.hint: You can stack case 'Saturday': case 'Sunday': return 'weekend'; and use default for weekdays.

lessons.title: Boolean returns and the early return pattern
lessons.summary: If a function only needs to return the result of a comparison, you can return the comparison itself — for example return a < b — instead of wrapping it in if / else that return true or false. The early return pattern exits a function as soon as an answer is known, which can make guard clauses clearer than deeply nested conditionals.

quiz.question: Which function body is equivalent to checking if a is equal to b and returning true or false?
choices: if (a === b) { return true; } else { return false; } and also return a === b;
Only a standalone if without a return
quiz.explanation: Returning the comparison directly is the shorter form taught in this chapter.

quiz.question: What is the idea behind an early return?
choices: Leave the function as soon as you know the result, often with a guard clause
Return only at the bottom of the file
Never use more than one return
quiz.explanation: Early returns avoid extra nesting when an input is invalid or a result is already decided.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite a function isShort(text) so it returns the boolean expression text.length < 5 directly, without an if statement.
exercise.hint: return text.length < 5;

lessons.title: Counting cards
lessons.summary: This challenge builds a blackjack card-counting function. When you see a low card the count goes up, a high card makes the count go down, and a middle value leaves the count unchanged. The function returns the current count plus a decision: 'Bet' if the count is positive, otherwise 'Hold'. Face cards and aces are treated as high cards.

quiz.question: In this card-counting function, what do low cards do to the count?
quiz.explanation: Beau says that when you see a low card the count goes up, and when you see a high card the count goes down.

quiz.question: What two pieces of information does the function return?
choices: The current count plus a 'Bet' or 'Hold' decision
The name of the card suit
quiz.explanation: The usual format is a string such as '5 Bet' or '-1 Hold'.

exercise.prompt: Write a cc(card) function that updates a global count and returns count + ' Bet' if the count is positive, otherwise count + ' Hold'. Decide your own mapping for 2–6, 7–9, and 10/J/Q/K/A.
exercise.hint: A switch with grouped cases is a clean way to classify each card.

lessons.title: Building and updating objects
lessons.summary: Objects are similar to arrays, except you access data with properties instead of numeric indexes. They are written with curly braces and name-value properties. You can read and update properties with dot notation (obj.x) or bracket notation (obj['x']). Brackets are required when the key is in a variable or is not a simple identifier. You can add new properties the same way, and delete removes a property.

quiz.question: When must you use bracket notation to access a property?
choices: Whenever the value is a number
When the property name is in a variable, or is not a valid identifier
quiz.explanation: obj[key] looks up whatever string is stored in key. Spaces or special characters also require brackets.

quiz.question: How do you remove a property named temp from an object user?
quiz.explanation: The delete operator removes an object property.

quiz.question: Which assignment adds a new property after the object already exists?
quiz.explanation: Assigning to a name that does not exist yet creates the property.

exercise.prompt: Create an object player with name and score. Update score, add a level property, then delete level and log the object.
exercise.hint: Use a mix of dot and bracket notation so you practice both.

lessons.title: Lookups and testing properties
lessons.summary: Objects can be thought of as a key-value storage, like a dictionary, and can replace a long switch statement as a lookup table: store answers under keys, then read result[key]. In the example, passing 'alpha' looks up 'Adams'. hasOwnProperty (or an equivalent check) tells you whether an object has a given property before you use it.

quiz.question: What is a lookup-table use of an object?
choices: Storing a value under a key so you can retrieve it instead of chaining many conditionals
quiz.explanation: For example, a map of abbreviations to full names.

quiz.question: How can you check whether an object has a property named 'city'?
quiz.explanation: This method returns true only if that property exists on the object itself.

exercise.prompt: Make a lookup object that maps 'MA' and 'CA' to state names. Write a function that returns the name, or 'not found' if the code is missing.
exercise.hint: Use hasOwnProperty or check whether lookup[code] is undefined.

lessons.title: Complex and nested structures
lessons.summary: A JavaScript object can store flexible data: strings, numbers, arrays, and even other objects. The lesson uses an array of album-like objects (myMusic) and then nested objects and nested arrays, showing how you chain dots and brackets to reach an inner value, such as collection.album.tracks[0].

quiz.question: How would you read the first track from record.tracks if tracks is an array?
quiz.explanation: Go to the tracks property, then take index 0.

quiz.question: Which structure is 'an array of objects'?
quiz.explanation: Each element of the array is an object.

exercise.prompt: Create an object library with a books array. Each book has title and year. Log the year of the second book.
exercise.hint: library.books[1].year

lessons.title: Record collection
lessons.summary: This coding challenge starts with a collection object where each record has an id and fields such as album, artist, and tracks (not every record has the same fields). You write a function that updates a record by id: if the given value is empty, delete that property; if the property is tracks, push onto an array (creating it if needed); otherwise set the property. Return the collection.

quiz.question: If the update value is an empty string, what should happen to that property?
choices: It should be deleted from the record
The whole record should be deleted
quiz.explanation: An empty value is the signal to remove the property.

quiz.question: What is special about the tracks property in this challenge?
choices: It is an array, and you may need to create it before pushing a new track
It must be stored as a string
quiz.explanation: If tracks does not exist yet, you create an array and then add the title.

exercise.prompt: Write updateRecords(collection, id, prop, value) with these rules: if value is '', delete the property; if prop is 'tracks', push value onto an array (creating it if needed); otherwise set the property to value. Return the collection.
exercise.hint: Handle the empty-value case first, then the tracks case, then the simple assignment.

lessons.title: While, for, and do...while loops

chapters.title: Odd Numbers With a For Loop
Count Backwards With a For Loop
Iterate Through an Array with a For Loop

lessons.summary: Loops run the same code multiple times. A while loop continues as long as its condition is true. A for loop packs initialization, condition, and increment into one line, and you can count up, count down, skip by two (for odd numbers), or walk an array with i < array.length. Nested loops are used for multi-dimensional arrays. A do...while loop runs the body at least once, then checks the condition.

quiz.question: When does a do...while loop check its condition?
choices: Before the first run of the body
After the body runs, so the body always runs at least once
Only when an error is thrown
quiz.explanation: That is the difference from a plain while loop.

quiz.question: Which for-loop header counts backwards from 10 to 0?
quiz.explanation: Start high, keep going while i is at least 0, and subtract one each time.

quiz.question: How do you typically iterate every item in an array named items?
quiz.explanation: Indexes run from 0 through length - 1.

exercise.prompt: Write a function sumArray(nums) that uses a for loop to add every number in the array and return the total. Then write a version of a loop that pushes the odd numbers from 1 to 9 into a new array.
exercise.hint: For odd numbers, try for (let i = 1; i <= 9; i += 2).

lessons.title: Profile lookup
lessons.summary: This challenge uses an array of contact objects, each with a first name, last name, number, and likes. You write a lookup function that loops through the contacts, finds a matching name, and returns the requested property if it exists, or a message if the name or the property does not exist. It combines loops, objects, and early returns.

quiz.question: What should the function do after it finds the matching contact name?
choices: Return the requested property if it exists, otherwise a 'no such property' style message
Continue looping to find later duplicates only
quiz.explanation: A name match is not enough; the property still has to exist.

quiz.question: What if no contact has the given name?
choices: Return a 'no such contact' style message
quiz.explanation: The loop finishing without a match means the name was not in the list.

exercise.prompt: Given an array of {firstName, lastName, number} contacts, write lookUp(name, prop) that returns the property, 'No such property', or 'No such contact'.
exercise.hint: Loop with a for loop, test firstName, then hasOwnProperty, and return after the loop if nothing matched.

lessons.title: Random numbers and parseInt
lessons.summary: Math.random() returns a decimal from 0 (inclusive) up to but not including 1. Multiplying by a range and using Math.floor gives a random whole number. parseInt converts a string to an integer, and an optional radix (such as 2) tells it which number base to use — for example parseInt('11', 2) is 3.

quiz.question: What range of values does Math.random() return?
choices: 0 inclusive up to, but not including, 1
quiz.explanation: It never reaches 1, which is why you multiply and floor to get integers in a range.

quiz.question: What does parseInt('11', 2) return?
quiz.explanation: The radix 2 means binary, and binary 11 is decimal 3.

quiz.question: Which expression gives a random integer from 0 to 9 inclusive?
quiz.explanation: random() * 10 goes from 0 up to almost 10, and floor maps that to 0–9.

exercise.prompt: Write randomRange(min, max) that returns a random integer between min and max inclusive. Also parse the binary string '1010' with parseInt and log the result.
exercise.hint: Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min. parseInt('1010', 2) is 10.

lessons.title: The ternary operator
lessons.summary: Beau presents the ternary operator as a one-line if / else expression: condition, then a question mark, then the value if true, then a colon, then the value if false. You can also nest ternaries for several branches, though readability matters. This is handy for simple value choices.

quiz.question: What does the expression score >= 50 ? 'pass' : 'fail' return when score is 40?
quiz.explanation: The condition is false, so the value after the colon is used.

quiz.question: Which structure is a valid nested ternary for a sign check?
quiz.explanation: Each : leads into the next condition or the final fallback.

exercise.prompt: Rewrite an if / else that returns 'adult' or 'minor' from an age as a single ternary. Then try a nested ternary that also returns 'infant' for ages under 2.
exercise.hint: age < 2 ? 'infant' : age < 18 ? 'minor' : 'adult'

lessons.title: let, const, and immutability

chapters.title: Mutate an Array Declared with const

lessons.summary: For a long time JavaScript only had var, but ES6 (2015) added let and const. let and const are block-scoped, unlike var, which is function-scoped and can be accidentally redeclared. const prevents reassignment of the binding, but objects and arrays held in const can still be mutated unless you freeze them. Object.freeze helps prevent changes to an object’s properties.

quiz.question: What is a key difference between var and let?
choices: let is block-scoped; var is function-scoped and can be redeclared in the same scope
let is only available inside classes
They behave identically in every case
quiz.explanation: This is the main reason the course switches beginners toward let and const.

quiz.question: If you declare const nums = [1, 2]; can you run nums.push(3)?
choices: No, const freezes the array contents
Yes. const prevents reassignment of nums, not mutation of the array itself
Only if you use var instead
quiz.explanation: nums = [] would fail, but changing items or pushing is allowed unless the array is frozen.

quiz.question: What does Object.freeze(obj) help with?
choices: It converts the object to a string
It prevents adding, removing, or changing the object’s properties (in strict usage)
quiz.explanation: The course uses freeze to prevent object mutation.

exercise.prompt: Declare a const array, mutate it with push, then try to reassign the variable and notice the error. After that, Object.freeze a settings object and try changing a property.
exercise.hint: In strict mode, assignments to frozen properties fail. Reassigning a const always fails.

lessons.title: Arrow functions, default, rest, and spread
lessons.summary: An anonymous function assigned to a variable can be rewritten as an arrow function, including implicit returns for a single expression. Default parameters fill in a value when an argument is missing. The rest operator gathers remaining arguments into an array, and the spread operator expands an array (or other iterable) into individual elements, which is useful for copying or combining arrays.

quiz.question: Which is an arrow function that doubles a number?
quiz.explanation: The parameter list comes before =>, and a single expression is returned automatically.

quiz.question: What does the rest operator do in function sum(...nums)?
choices: It forces nums to be a number
It collects all arguments into an array named nums
It spreads nums into the caller
quiz.explanation: Rest is on the parameter side; spread is the similar-looking syntax used in calls or array literals.

quiz.question: What does const copy = [...original] do?
choices: Creates a shallow copy of the original array
quiz.explanation: Spread expands the items into a new array literal.

exercise.prompt: Write an arrow function sumAll(...nums) that returns the total of all arguments. Then create a new array with spread that starts with 0 and includes all of [1, 2, 3].
exercise.hint: sumAll can use a loop or nums.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0). The new array is [0, ...[1, 2, 3]].

lessons.title: Destructuring and template literals
lessons.summary: Destructuring assignment is a syntax for neatly taking values from an object or array and assigning them to variables, including nested values and function parameters. You can also gather remaining items with rest. Template literals use backticks and ${expression} to build strings across multiple lines without manual concatenation.

quiz.question: What does const {name} = user; do?
choices: Creates a new object named name
Declares a variable name and sets it to user.name
quiz.explanation: Object destructuring copies the matching property into a new variable.

quiz.question: Which string uses a template literal correctly?
quiz.explanation: Backticks are required for interpolation.

quiz.question: What does const [first, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4]; assign to rest?
quiz.explanation: first takes 1; the rest operator gathers the remaining items.

exercise.prompt: Given const person = {name: 'Ada', city: 'London', year: 1815}; destructure name and city, then log a template literal that uses both. Also destructure the first item of [10, 20, 30].
exercise.hint: const {name, city} = person; console.log(`${name} lived in ${city}.`); const [first] = [10, 20, 30];

lessons.title: Classes, shorthand fields, and getters
lessons.summary: ES6 added support for easily defining object literals: simple fields copy an existing variable into a same-named property, and concise method syntax goes inside the object. class syntax is a clearer way to write constructor functions and methods. Getters and setters let you read or update a property through methods, which is useful for computed or guarded values.

quiz.question: What is the shorthand for { name: name } when the variable is already called name?
quiz.explanation: Simple fields copy an existing variable into a same-named property.

quiz.question: In class syntax, where do you usually initialize instance data?
choices: In a method named init only
quiz.explanation: constructor receives arguments and typically assigns them to this.

quiz.question: What does a getter let you do?
choices: Call a method as if it were a property, such as obj.area
quiz.explanation: You define get area() { ... } and then read obj.area.

exercise.prompt: Write a class Rectangle with a constructor for width and height, a getter area, and a setter that updates width. Create one instance and log its area.
exercise.hint: get area() { return this.width * this.height; }

lessons.title: import and export
lessons.summary: In the past, people used require to pull in code from other files. Now you export a function, class, or constant from one file and import it in another, either as a named export or a default export. The lesson shows named imports with curly braces and importing a default export, and it is the closing chapter of the video.

quiz.question: What older function does this lesson contrast with import and export?
quiz.explanation: Beau starts by contrasting the older require function with the newer import and export syntax.

quiz.question: How do you import a named export add from a file './math.js'?
quiz.explanation: Named imports use curly braces and the exported name.

exercise.prompt: In a practice file, export a function shout(text) as a named export and imagine importing it with import { shout } from './shout.js'. If you use this app’s dev server, you can try it as a small extra module later.
exercise.hint: export function shout(text) { return text + '!'; }
